explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already come a long way. In earlier units you built three thinking skills, and now you meet a fourth. Here are the six skills of Global Perspectives once more, so you can see where you are:

This unit is all about the fourth skill: Reflection. The first three skills point outward, at a topic in the world. Reflection is different. It points inward, at you. It asks you to stop and think about how you learn, what helps you, and how your own thinking has grown and changed. That may sound unusual, but it is one of the most powerful skills a learner can have.

Why does reflection matter beyond school? Think about how adults get better at anything. A nurse who thinks back on a hard day works out what to do better next time. A coach who reviews a lost match spots what the team must practise. A shopkeeper who notices which goods did not sell changes the order next month. None of them is simply working harder; they are reflecting, then improving. The learner who reflects well this year will keep improving for the rest of their life, in every subject and every job.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how your ideas have changed.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand you.

explainers.title: What makes reflection special
explainers.body:
Most of the time at school, you are asked about what you learned: the facts, the answers, the findings. Reflection asks a different and deeper question. It asks how you learned it. What did you do that worked? What got in your way? When did your mind change, and why?

Here is a simple way to feel the difference. Imagine you have just finished a piece of research.

Both thoughts are useful, but only the second one makes you a better learner. In this unit you will practise having more of those 'how' thoughts, on purpose, until they become a habit.

Reflection is already part of life around you, even if nobody calls it that. After the rains, a farmer near Hargeisa thinks about which field drained well and which flooded, then plants differently next season. A shopkeeper in Berbera notices which goods sold before a festival and orders more of them next year. A footballer replays a missed goal in her mind and practises that exact kick. In each case the person is not just remembering; they are learning from the memory. That is reflection, and this unit simply teaches you to do it on purpose, about your own learning.
bullets: A what thought is: 'I found out that many families walk a long way for water.'
A how thought is: 'I learned most when I stopped rushing and asked my AI tutor to check my questions. I need to do that earlier next time.'

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in Ehel Academy's self-paced way, and reflection fits this way of learning perfectly, because reflection is something only you can do about your own mind. Three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were often told to 'discuss with a partner' or asked 'does your partner agree?'. In our model, your AI tutor is that partner, ready at any hour. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a real conversation. Say your ideas out loud or type them, and let the tutor ask you questions back.

One part of Reflection is about teamwork, and teamwork needs other people. In our model, team tasks happen in your teacher sessions and in group projects your teacher arranges, so you will still work with real classmates. You then reflect on that teamwork afterwards, in your own time, with this book and your AI tutor to guide you.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. Reflection needs quiet thinking time, and self-paced learning gives you exactly that.

Your AI tutor, available 24 hours a day. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as a study partner who helps you notice things about your own learning that are hard to see alone.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your reflections, take part in team tasks, and hear how other learners think and work.

explainers.title: Meet Leo, our reflector for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each idea clear, we will follow one Year 7 learner through the whole unit. His name is Leo, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. You may remember Amal from your very first unit; Leo sits a few desks away from where she did.

Leo's Challenge topic is sugary drinks in school. When the unit begins, Leo has a strong opinion: he loves fizzy sugary drinks, and he thinks it would be unfair and pointless for the school to limit them. That is his personal perspective at the start. Hold on to that, because one of the most interesting things you will watch in this unit is how Leo's view slowly changes as he learns, researches, and listens to other people.

As you meet each part of Reflection, you will see exactly what Leo notices about his own learning, his teamwork, and his changing opinion. By the end, he will be able to explain not just what he thinks, but how and why his thinking changed. You will be doing the very same thing with your own Challenge topic.

explainers.title: Your Challenge, and looking back on it
explainers.body:
All through Global Perspectives you have been building a Challenge: a global topic that also matters right where you live. In the earlier units you researched it, analysed it and evaluated it. In this unit you do something new with it: you look back on the whole journey and notice how you, and your ideas, have grown.

If you are just joining the Challenge now, that is fine. Pick a topic that matters in your area, such as one of these:

You will keep returning to your Challenge in this unit, but with reflection questions rather than research questions. Instead of asking 'what is true about my topic?', you will ask 'how has my thinking about my topic changed, and what helped me learn?'.
bullets: Clean water for every family
Healthy food and drinks, and good school meals
Plastic waste in our streets and on our coasts
Road safety on busy streets
Renewable energy, such as solar power
Protecting wildlife, such as sea turtles on the Berbera coast
Education for all, including girls staying in school

explainers.title: What is reflection, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think reflection just means saying whether you enjoyed a lesson. Real reflection is more useful than that. Reflection is stopping to think honestly about how you learn and how your thinking changes, so that you can improve.

A reflective learner does four things again and again:

Notice that reflection is not about being hard on yourself. It is not a list of everything you did wrong. A good reflection is honest but kind: it sees what went well, sees what could be better, and turns that into a plan. Being able to say 'I found this hard, and here is how I will improve' is a sign of a strong learner, not a weak one.
bullets: Looks back at what they did and how they did it.
Notices what helped their learning and what got in the way.
Notices how their ideas or their opinion changed, and why.
Decides one thing to do differently next time.

explainers.title: Keep a reflection journal
explainers.body:
The single best habit for this unit is to keep a reflection journal. This can be a notebook or a document where, after each piece of work, you write a few honest lines about your learning. It is not a diary of your whole day; it is a record of how you learned and how your thinking changed.

A reflection journal matters for three reasons. First, thinking becomes clearer when you write it down; a feeling in your head turns into a sentence you can actually use. Second, it shows your growth over time, so that weeks later you can read an old entry and see how far you have come. Third, it gives you real examples to talk about in your teacher sessions and to use in the self-assessment tables in this unit.

A good journal entry does not need to be long. Three or four honest sentences are enough. Use these prompts to get started:

explainers.title: When should you stop and reflect?
explainers.body:
Many learners think reflection only happens at the very end, once everything is finished. In truth, the strongest learners reflect at three different moments, and each one helps in a different way:

You do not need long for any of these. A reflection can take thirty seconds. The skill is not spending hours thinking; it is building the habit of pausing at the right moments instead of rushing blindly on. As you work through this unit, try catching yourself at all three: before, during, and after.
bullets: Before you start, look back at the last time you did something similar. What worked? What will you do differently this time?
During the work, pause when you feel stuck or confused. Ask yourself what is getting in the way right now, and change your approach.
After you finish, look back at the whole task and turn what you noticed into a target for next time.

explainers.title: Knowing your strengths and your areas to develop
explainers.body:
Reflection starts with knowing yourself as a learner. Every learner has personal strengths, the things they are already good at, and areas to develop, the things they are still working to get better at. Knowing both is a strength in itself.

Here are four learning behaviours. As you read them, notice which feel like your strengths and which you find harder:

None of these makes you a 'good' or 'bad' learner. They are simply things you can grow. An area to develop is not a weakness to hide; it is the exact place where you have the most room to improve. In fact, naming an area to develop is one of the smartest things a learner can do, because you cannot improve something you have not noticed.
bullets: Listening to the ideas of others without interrupting.
Asking for help when you are stuck, instead of giving up quietly.
Asking questions to understand something better.
Giving your opinion clearly, even when it is different from others.

explainers.title: Noticing what helps and what blocks your learning
explainers.body:
Two learners can do exactly the same task and learn very different amounts, because different things help and block each of them. A huge part of reflection is simply noticing your own helpers and blockers, so you can use more of one and less of the other.

Helpers and blockers are different for everyone, but here are some common ones to look out for:

The trick is to catch these in the moment and write them in your journal. Over a few weeks you will see a clear pattern of what makes learning easier for you, and that pattern is pure gold.
bullets: Helpers might be: a quiet space, breaking a big task into small parts, talking an idea through with your AI tutor, seeing a worked example first, or taking a short break.
Blockers might be: noise and interruptions, rushing to finish, trying to hold too much in your head at once, being afraid to ask for help, or giving up at the first hard moment.

explainers.title: Reflecting on teamwork: the benefits and the challenges
explainers.body:
Some of the best learning happens with other people. In Global Perspectives you will sometimes work in a team towards a shared outcome, such as a short video or a podcast about your topic. Reflection asks you to look back on that teamwork and notice both its benefits and its challenges. This is Cambridge objective 4.2.

First, it helps to be clear about what real teamwork is:

But teamwork also brings real challenges, and pretending it is always easy would not be honest reflection:

A reflective teammate does not just complain about the challenges. They think, 'What did our team do about this, and what could I do differently next time?'. That is the difference between a bad experience and a lesson learned.
bullets: More ideas, so no one has to struggle alone.
The workload is shared more fairly.
Team members support and encourage each other.
Each person's strengths add to the whole, so the team can do more than any one person.
Tasks can be finished faster.
People can disagree about ideas.
There can be conflict over who does what.
Personalities can clash.
One team member may be absent, or may not do their share.

explainers.title: Your contribution to a team, and setting a target
explainers.body:
It is easy to talk about how a team did as a whole. Reflection asks the harder, more honest question: what did you, personally, contribute? Then it asks you to set a target to improve your contribution next time. This is Cambridge objective 4.1.

Your contribution is whatever you brought to the shared outcome. It might be an idea, a skill, hard work on one part, keeping everyone calm, or making sure the team stayed organised. Being honest about your contribution means naming both what you did well and where you could have done more.

Then you set a target. A good target is small and clear, and you can tell when you have reached it. Think of it as a friendly promise to yourself. You can check any target against four quick questions, a simple version of what people call a SMART target:
bullets: Specific — does it say exactly what I will do?
Measurable — will I be able to tell when I have done it?
Achievable — can I really do it?
Realistic in time — can I do it in the time I have?

explainers.title: Your personal perspective, and how it can change
explainers.body:
Now we reach the heart of Reflection. A personal perspective is your own point of view on an issue, shaped by who you are, where you live, your experiences, and what matters to you. It is not the same as a local perspective (the view shared across your community) or a national or global perspective (the view of your whole country, or the wider world). Your personal perspective is simply yours.

Take the example of sugary drinks. Your personal perspective might be that you love them, because you grew up drinking them at family celebrations. The local perspective in your neighbourhood might be that they are a cheap treat everyone enjoys. The national perspective might focus on the health of children across the country, and the global perspective might look at how much sugar is sold worldwide. The same issue looks different at each level, and noticing that is part of thinking clearly about your own view.

Here is the powerful part. Cambridge objective 4.3 is about noticing how your personal perspective may have changed after you did research or heard other people's perspectives. In everyday life, changing your mind is sometimes treated as a bad thing, as if it means you were wrong or weak. In Global Perspectives, it is the opposite. Changing or developing your view because you met good reasons and new voices is a sign of a strong, open mind.

A simple frame helps you notice and explain a change in your perspective:

That little word 'because' is the most important part, because it shows the reason your mind moved. A reflection without a reason is just an opinion; a reflection with a 'because' shows real learning.
bullets: Before, I thought ...
Now, I think ...
This changed because ...

explainers.title: Naming the skills you have learnt or improved
explainers.body:
After any activity, a reflective learner can name at least one skill they learnt and one skill they improved, and link these to their personal strengths and areas to develop. This is Cambridge objective 4.4. It turns a finished task into a clear sense of 'I can now do something I could not do before'.

There is a small but useful difference between the two:

Naming these skills is not showing off. It is honest stock-taking. When you can say exactly what you gained, you also see more clearly what to work on next, and that is how learning keeps moving forward.
bullets: A skill you learnt is something quite new to you, that you could barely do before.
A skill you improved is something you could already do a little, and are now better at.

explainers.title: How Reflection strengthens the other five skills
explainers.body:
Reflection is not a skill you use once and put away. It quietly makes every other Global Perspectives skill stronger, because after each one you stop, notice, and improve.

This is why reflection sits in the middle of your learning, not at the end. Every time you finish something and take a moment to think about how it went, you are making your next attempt better.
bullets: Research gets better when you reflect on which of your questions and sources actually worked.
Analysis gets better when you notice which ways of breaking a topic apart helped you most.
Evaluation gets better when you reflect on times your first judgement turned out to be wrong.
Collaboration gets much better when you honestly reflect on how you worked in a team.
Communication gets better when you look back at which explanations your audience understood, and which confused them.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the reflection cycle
explainers.body:
You have now met every part of Reflection in this unit. They fit together into one simple cycle you can use after any piece of work:

Remember the three stages the source of this unit describes: you are starting to reflect, then developing your reflection, then getting better at it. Nobody masters reflection in a day. It grows, quietly, every time you go round the cycle.
bullets: Pause at the end of a task, instead of rushing straight on.
Look back at what you did and how you did it.
Notice what helped your learning and what blocked it.
Notice how your perspective changed, and say why (the 'because').
Name one skill you learnt or improved, and how it fits your strengths.
Set one small, clear target for next time.
Write it all in your reflection journal, so the learning is not lost.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Collaboration. It is a natural partner to Reflection, because you have already begun thinking about how you work with other people. In Collaboration you will learn to plan, share roles, handle disagreement and reach a shared outcome on purpose. The reflective habits you build now, especially the honest way you look at your own contribution, will make you a far stronger teammate. Well done for having the courage to turn your thinking inward. That is where real growth begins.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: In Research, Analysis and Evaluation, the topic is the star.
In Reflection, you are the star.
The point is not to learn more facts about water or waste. The point is to understand how you learn, and how your own view of an issue can change, so you can keep getting better.

bigIdeas.title: Strengths and areas to develop go together
lines: Often your greatest strength and your area to develop are two sides of the same thing.
Being confident can make listening harder. Being careful can make you slow to speak up.
A reflective learner uses their strength and works gently on the other side.

bigIdeas.title: Teamwork is, and is not
lines: Teamwork is a group working together towards a shared outcome, with a positive atmosphere, supporting each other and combining their strengths.
Teamwork is not everyone working alone and only joining their parts at the end.
Teamwork is not one person forcing their own ideas onto the group.
When teamwork goes well, the benefits are real:

bigIdeas.title: A weak target and a strong target
lines: Weak target: I will be better at teamwork. This is too vague to act on.
Strong target: I will offer to do one clear job at the start of our next team task.
The strong target tells you exactly what to do, and you can tell when you have done it.

bigIdeas.title: Reflecting fairly on views that differ
lines: In your class, learners hold many different views. One classmate may fast during one tradition's fasting period; another may look forward to a different festival; another may follow no faith at all.
A good reflector listens to all of these fairly and asks how each person's experiences shaped their perspective, without deciding one is right and the others wrong.
Being fair to many perspectives, and noticing how they shift your own, is exactly what Global Perspectives is about.

bigIdeas.title: How reflection activities are different
lines: In other units, the activities asked about a topic in the world.
Here, most activities ask about you: how you learn, how you work with others, and how your ideas have changed.
There are no wrong answers. An honest not there yet is worth more than a dishonest achieved.

bigIdeas.title: Remember
lines: An area to develop is not a weakness to feel bad about.
It is simply the place where you have the most room to grow.
Naming it honestly is one of the smartest things a learner can do.

bigIdeas.title: The reflection is not about the text
lines: The point of this activity is not to become an expert on the topic.
The point is to notice how you took the ideas in, and what helped you understand them.
That is the difference between reading and truly learning.

bigIdeas.title: Be honest about your own part
lines: It is easy to see what others did wrong in a team.
Real reflection means looking just as honestly at your own contribution.
Name what you did well and where you could have done more.

bigIdeas.title: Skills grow across subjects
lines: The skills you name here, such as asking better questions or listening carefully, do not only help in Global Perspectives.
They travel with you into every subject, and into life beyond school.
That is why naming them, and knowing you have them, matters so much.

bigIdeas.title: Growth is easy to miss
lines: Because you improve a little at a time, you rarely feel yourself getting better.
Comparing old work with new work makes that hidden growth visible.
Almost every learner is surprised by how far they have come.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 4 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Reflection.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, what is the difference between what I learned and how I learned it?
Then tell the tutor about one time you changed your mind about something, and ask it why changing your mind can be a good thing.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think reflection means.
Ask the tutor: Is my definition missing anything important?
Then tell it about one recent task, and practise turning a what thought into a how thought about your own learning.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Write your very first reflection journal entry, using the five prompts above.
Read it to your AI tutor and ask: Is this a real reflection, or am I only describing what I did?
Ask the tutor for one question it would add to my journal to make me think more deeply.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which of the four learning behaviours are your strengths and which you find harder.
Give one real example for each, from your own recent work.
Ask the tutor: Based on what I said, what one area would be most useful for me to develop first?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a recent lesson: what helped your learning and what got in the way?
Ask it to help you name one clear helper and one clear blocker.
Ask the tutor for one practical way to reduce your blocker next time.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a time you worked in a team, in or out of school.
Ask it to help you name one clear benefit and one clear challenge you experienced.
Ask the tutor: what is one thing I could do to handle that challenge better next time?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about your contribution to a recent team or group task, honestly.
Ask it to help you turn a vague goal into one small, clear target.
Ask the tutor to check your target against the four questions: specific, measurable, achievable, and realistic in time.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor what you thought about your Challenge topic at the very start of your Global Perspectives journey.
Then tell it what you think now, and use the word because to explain what changed your mind.
Ask the tutor: Did I really change my view, or did I just learn more reasons for the view I already had? Both are worth noticing.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a task you finished recently.
Ask it to help you name one skill you learnt and one skill you improved during that task.
Ask the tutor how these skills connect to your personal strengths and the area you want to develop.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your first journal entry to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is this honest reflection, or am I being too hard or too easy on myself?
Ask the tutor to suggest one question I should ask myself at the end of every journal entry.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers, with your examples, to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your examples really show a strength or an area to develop.
Ask the tutor: which area to develop should I focus on first, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your helpers, blockers and plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your plan is realistic and small enough to actually do.
Ask the tutor for one more idea to reduce your biggest blocker.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to give you a short text about a global topic, then read it.
Tell the tutor the main message and one thing you now understand.
Ask it: from the way I talked about the text, which learning behaviours did I use well, and which could I use more?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your before, now and because sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your because really explains what changed your mind.
Ask the tutor: did I change my whole view, or did I make my first view fairer and deeper? Both are real reflection.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about your team task, using your four answers.
Ask it to help you see the challenge from another team member's point of view.
Ask the tutor: what is one thing I could do to be a stronger teammate next time?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two targets to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check each one against the four questions: specific, measurable, achievable, and realistic in time.
Ask the tutor to help you sharpen any target that is too vague.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the skill you learnt and the skill you improved.
Ask it whether these connect well to the strengths and area to develop you named in Activity 2.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill worth building next, and why.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your early piece of work to your AI tutor, and what you would change now.
Ask it to help you name exactly which skills have grown since then.
Ask the tutor: what does this growth suggest I should work on next?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three Challenge sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking has changed since you started.
Ask the tutor to suggest one reflection habit to carry into the Collaboration unit.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more scenario like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your rewritten reflections and targets to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether each reflection now says how you learned, and whether each target is small and clear.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to improve any answer you found hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking about learning changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one reflection habit to focus on in the next unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A family conversation
lines: Ask a family member to tell you about a time they changed their mind about something important.
What made them change it? New information, a new experience, or hearing someone else's story?
Bring their answer to your next teacher session. Grown-ups change their minds too, and hearing how they do it helps you understand your own reflection.

speakingPrompts.title: Bring it to your teacher session
lines: Save your before, now and because sentences.
Share them in your next teacher session and listen to how other learners' views changed.
Hearing different journeys often helps you understand your own even better.

speakingPrompts.title: Share your targets
lines: Write your two targets on the first page of your reflection journal.
Share them in your next teacher session, and ask a family member to remind you of them during the week.
A target you have said out loud to someone else is far more likely to happen.

toolkit.title: The reflection cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever you have just finished, good reflection follows the same simple cycle. Come back to this list whenever you are not sure where to start. With practice it becomes automatic, and you will find yourself running through it in your head without even trying.
items: Pause: stop at the end of a task instead of rushing on.
Look back: what did I do, and how did I do it?
Notice helpers and blockers: what made learning easier or harder?
Notice change: how did my perspective change, and why (the 'because')?
Name skills: what did I learn or improve, and how does it fit my strengths?
Set a target: one small, clear thing to do differently next time.
Write it down: record it in my reflection journal so it is not lost.

toolkit.title: The Reflection skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Reflection is stopping to think honestly about how you learn and how your thinking changes, so that you can improve. It is not just saying whether you enjoyed a task. Real reflection means noticing what helped and blocked your learning, noticing how your own view of an issue grew or changed, naming what you gained, and turning all of that into a clear plan for next time.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always be honest but kind with yourself, because a reflection that only blames you is not useful, and one that only praises you does not help you grow. Second, always finish with a because and a target, because the reason your mind changed and the plan for next time are what turn thinking into real improvement.

toolkit.title: Three good moments to reflect
toolkit.intro: Reflection is not only for the end of a task. The strongest learners pause at three moments, and each helps in a different way.
items: Before a task: look back at last time. What worked, and what will I change?
During a task: when I feel stuck, what is getting in the way right now?
After a task: what did I learn about my learning, and what is my target for next time?

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 7 Reflection objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong reflection looks like at this stage. Here are the official Reflection objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Explain personal contribution to teamwork and identify targets for improvement.
Say what you brought to a team, and set a clear target to do better next time.
Consider the benefits and challenges of teamwork experienced when working together to achieve a shared outcome.
Notice the good things and the hard things about working as a team towards one result.
Consider ways that personal perspective on an issue may have changed as a result of conducting research or exploring different perspectives.
Notice how your own view of an issue changed after you researched it or heard other people's views, and say why.
Identify skills learnt or improved during an activity and relate to personal strengths and areas for improvement.
Name a skill you learnt or got better at, and link it to what you are good at and what you want to develop.

toolkit.title: Template: A reflection journal entry
toolkit.intro: Copy this simple frame after each task. Three or four honest sentences are plenty.

rows: Date and what I worked on
What helped my learning most?
What got in the way, and what will I try instead?
Did my opinion change at all? How, and why?
One small target for next time

toolkit.title: Template: The before and after viewpoint frame
toolkit.intro:
Use this frame to notice and explain how your personal perspective has changed. The 'because' is the most important line.

If your view did not change, use the same frame to explain why it stayed the same, for example: 'because my research kept giving me the same answer'. A view that survives good research and other perspectives is stronger for it, so an unchanged view with a clear because is still real reflection.
items: Before, I thought ...
Now, I think ...
This changed because ... (name the research, experience or person that moved your thinking).

toolkit.title: Template: Setting a target (SMART-lite)
toolkit.intro:
A good target is a small, clear promise to yourself. Check every target against these four questions.

Write your target in this shape: Area to improve ______. What I will do ______. Aim for one small thing you could start tomorrow, not a huge promise you cannot keep.

rows: Specific
Does it say exactly what I will do?
Measurable
Will I be able to tell when I have done it?
Achievable
Can I really do this?
Realistic in time
Can I do it in the time I have?

toolkit.title: Template: Reflecting on teamwork
toolkit.intro:
After any team task, work through these five prompts to reflect fairly on the team and on your own part in it.

The hardest and most useful prompt is the third one, about your own contribution. It is always easier to see what teammates did wrong than to look honestly at your own part. A reflection that names your own contribution fairly, both the good and the could-do-better, is a sign of a mature learner.
items: One benefit our team experienced was ...
One challenge our team faced was ...
My own contribution to the shared outcome was ...
One thing we did, or could have done, about the challenge was ...
My target for the next team task is ...

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for reflection
toolkit.intro:
Use these to get your reflections started. They work in your journal, your teacher sessions, and with your AI tutor. If you ever feel stuck staring at a blank page, pick any starter below and simply finish the sentence; the thinking usually follows once you begin to write.

Noticing how you learn:

Noticing how your view changed:

Reflecting on teamwork and skills:
items: I learned best when ...
What helped me most was ...
What got in my way was ...
Next time I will ...
Before, I thought ... but now I think ...
My view changed because ...
Hearing ... helped me see ...
I still think ..., but now I also understand ...
What I contributed to the team was ...
One benefit and one challenge of our teamwork were ...
A skill I learnt was ..., and a skill I improved was ...
My target for next time is ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this a strong reflection?
checklists.intro: Tick each one. If you cannot tick them all, add the missing part.
items: Honest — it says what went well and what could be better, kindly.
About how, not just what — it describes how I learned, not only what I did.
Has a because — if my view changed, it says why.
Names something gained — a skill I learnt or improved.
Ends in a target — one small, clear thing to do next time.

challenge.intro:
Pull your reflection together by completing these three sentences about your Challenge topic, in your own words. You may have met them before; the point is to see how your answers have grown.

Keep this checkpoint safe in your reflection journal. Reading it again at the end of the next unit will show you, in your own handwriting, exactly how far your thinking has travelled. Most learners are surprised, and quietly proud, when they see the distance between where they started and where they are now.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Start your reflection journal
activities.label: Activity 1: Start your reflection journal
activities.intro: Every reflective learner needs somewhere to think on paper. Start your journal now and you will use it in every activity that follows. It can be a paper notebook or a document on a device, whichever you will actually keep coming back to.
steps: At the top of a fresh page or document, write today's date and the title 'My Reflection Journal'.
Write two or three sentences about how you feel as a learner right now: what are you good at, and what do you find hard?
Write one thing you hope to get better at during this unit.

boxes.title: If you are not sure what to write
lines: I learn best when ...
I find it hard when ...
One thing I want to improve is ...

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your first journal entry to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is this honest reflection, or am I being too hard or too easy on myself?
Ask the tutor to suggest one question I should ask myself at the end of every journal entry.

activities.title: Your strengths and your areas to develop
activities.label: Activity 2: Your strengths and your areas to develop
activities.intro:
You cannot improve what you have not noticed. In this activity you take an honest look at yourself as a learner. Nobody is only strengths or only areas to develop; every learner is a mix, and knowing your own mix is the whole point.

Think about these four learning behaviours: listening to others, asking for help, asking questions, and giving your opinion. For each one, decide honestly whether it is a strength of yours or an area to develop.
steps: Write the four behaviours as a list.
Next to each, write 'strength' or 'area to develop', and one real example from your own work.
Choose the single area to develop you think would help you most, and write one sentence on why.

boxes.title: Remember
lines: An area to develop is not a weakness to feel bad about.
It is simply the place where you have the most room to grow.
Naming it honestly is one of the smartest things a learner can do.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers, with your examples, to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your examples really show a strength or an area to develop.
Ask the tutor: which area to develop should I focus on first, and why?

activities.title: What helped and what blocked my learning
activities.label: Activity 3: What helped and what blocked my learning
activities.intro:
Different things help and block each learner. This activity helps you spot your own pattern, which is one of the most useful things you can know about yourself. What blocks one person, such as background noise, might not bother another at all, so there are no right answers here, only your honest answers.

Think back over your recent Global Perspectives work: your research, your analysis, your evaluation. Try to remember specific moments when learning felt easy, and moments when it felt hard.
steps: Write down three things that helped your learning (for example: a quiet space, a worked example, talking to your AI tutor).
Write down three things that blocked your learning (for example: noise, rushing, being afraid to ask for help).
Choose your biggest helper and your biggest blocker, and write one sentence on each.
Write one small plan to use more of your helper and less of your blocker.

boxes.title: A model answer from Layla
lines: Biggest helper: I learn most when I break a task into small parts.
Biggest blocker: I rush when I am tired, and then I make careless mistakes.
My plan: I will do my hardest work earlier in the day, in small steps, and take a short break between them.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your helpers, blockers and plan to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your plan is realistic and small enough to actually do.
Ask the tutor for one more idea to reduce your biggest blocker.

activities.title: Reflect on how you learn from a text
activities.label: Activity 4: Reflect on how you learn from a text
activities.intro: Reading and thinking about a text is a good chance to watch your own learning happen. In this activity you read a short text, then reflect on how reading it changed what you understand. Ask your AI tutor to give you a short text (three or four small paragraphs) about any global topic, such as clean water, plastic waste, or healthy food.
steps: Read the text once, then write the main message in one sentence.
Write one thing the text made you understand that you did not understand before.
Reflect: did reading and then talking it through with your AI tutor help your learning? Answer yes or no, and explain why.
Reflect: which of your learning behaviours did you use here, such as asking questions or asking for help?

boxes.title: The reflection is not about the text
lines: The point of this activity is not to become an expert on the topic.
The point is to notice how you took the ideas in, and what helped you understand them.
That is the difference between reading and truly learning.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to give you a short text about a global topic, then read it.
Tell the tutor the main message and one thing you now understand.
Ask it: from the way I talked about the text, which learning behaviours did I use well, and which could I use more?

activities.title: How my viewpoint changed
activities.label: Activity 5: How my viewpoint changed
activities.intro:
This is the most important reflection activity in the unit. You will trace how your personal perspective on your Challenge topic has changed since you began, and explain why. Remember, changing or developing your view because you met good reasons is a sign of a strong, open mind, not a weak one.

Look back at what you thought about your topic at the very start of Global Perspectives, then at what you think now. Take your time, and be honest even if your view has barely moved.

If your view has not changed much, that is fine too. Then explain why it stayed the same: perhaps your research kept giving you the same answer, which is also worth noticing. Either way, the 'because' is what matters.
steps: Complete this sentence: 'Before, I thought ...'.
Complete this sentence: 'Now, I think ...'.
Complete this sentence: 'This changed because ...'. Name the research, experience or person that moved your thinking.
Write one sentence about how it feels to notice your own mind changing.

boxes.title: A model answer about a changed viewpoint
lines: Before, I thought plastic bags were fine and banning them was silly.
Now, I think we should use far fewer of them, though a sudden total ban might hurt market sellers.
This changed because I watched bags block a drain after the rains, and I interviewed a seller who explained her side.
It feels strange but good to notice my mind changing when I meet real reasons.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your before, now and because sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your because really explains what changed your mind.
Ask the tutor: did I change my whole view, or did I make my first view fairer and deeper? Both are real reflection.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher session
lines: Save your before, now and because sentences.
Share them in your next teacher session and listen to how other learners' views changed.
Hearing different journeys often helps you understand your own even better.

activities.title: Reflecting on a team task
activities.label: Activity 6: Reflecting on a team task
activities.intro: Think about a time you worked in a team, in a teacher session, a group project, or even outside school, such as a chore shared with your family. This activity helps you reflect on the benefits and challenges, and on your own part in it. If you have not done a team task recently, your teacher will set one up in a live session; you can come back and complete this activity afterwards.
steps: Write one real benefit your team experienced (for example: more ideas, shared work, support).
Write one real challenge your team faced (for example: disagreement, uneven work, a clash).
Write honestly what you personally contributed to the shared outcome.
Write one thing your team did, or could have done, to handle the challenge better.

boxes.title: Be honest about your own part
lines: It is easy to see what others did wrong in a team.
Real reflection means looking just as honestly at your own contribution.
Name what you did well and where you could have done more.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about your team task, using your four answers.
Ask it to help you see the challenge from another team member's point of view.
Ask the tutor: what is one thing I could do to be a stronger teammate next time?

activities.title: Set your improvement targets
activities.label: Activity 7: Set your improvement targets
activities.intro:
Reflection is only powerful when it leads to action. In this activity you turn what you have noticed into two clear targets. A good target is small, clear, and you can tell when you have reached it. Think of each target as a friendly promise to yourself, not a heavy rule.

Look back at Activities 2, 3 and 6, where you thought about your strengths, your helpers and blockers, and your teamwork. Choose two areas you most want to improve.
steps: Target 1. Area to improve: ______. What I will do: ______.
Target 2. Area to improve: ______. What I will do: ______.
Check each target against four questions: is it specific, can I measure it, can I achieve it, and can I do it in the time I have?

boxes.title: A model target
lines: Area to improve: I rarely ask for help when I am stuck.
What I will do: In my next research task, I will ask my AI tutor for help the moment I am stuck for more than five minutes.
This is specific, I will know when I have done it, and it is realistic.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two targets to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check each one against the four questions: specific, measurable, achievable, and realistic in time.
Ask the tutor to help you sharpen any target that is too vague.

boxes.title: Share your targets
lines: Write your two targets on the first page of your reflection journal.
Share them in your next teacher session, and ask a family member to remind you of them during the week.
A target you have said out loud to someone else is far more likely to happen.

activities.title: Name what you have learnt
activities.label: Activity 8: Name what you have learnt
activities.intro: Finish by taking honest stock of what you have gained. Naming your skills turns a pile of finished tasks into a clear sense of growth, and it points you towards what to build next.
steps: Write one skill you have learnt during Global Perspectives, something you could barely do before.
Write one skill you have improved, something you could already do a little.
Link each to yourself: which of your personal strengths helped, and which area to develop does it touch?

boxes.title: Skills grow across subjects
lines: The skills you name here, such as asking better questions or listening carefully, do not only help in Global Perspectives.
They travel with you into every subject, and into life beyond school.
That is why naming them, and knowing you have them, matters so much.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the skill you learnt and the skill you improved.
Ask it whether these connect well to the strengths and area to develop you named in Activity 2.
Ask the tutor to suggest one skill worth building next, and why.

activities.title: Look back at your earlier work
activities.label: Activity 9: Look back at your earlier work
activities.intro:
Reflection becomes real when you can see your own growth with your own eyes. In this activity you compare something you made near the start of Global Perspectives with what you could do now.

Find an early piece of your work, such as your first research question, an early set of notes, or your very first Challenge checkpoint.
steps: Read it carefully. Write one thing you did well, even back then.
Write one thing you would now do differently, and why.
Write one sentence finishing: 'When I look at my early work, I can see that I have grown in ...'.
Add this reflection to your journal, so your growth is recorded.

boxes.title: Growth is easy to miss
lines: Because you improve a little at a time, you rarely feel yourself getting better.
Comparing old work with new work makes that hidden growth visible.
Almost every learner is surprised by how far they have come.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your early piece of work to your AI tutor, and what you would change now.
Ask it to help you name exactly which skills have grown since then.
Ask the tutor: what does this growth suggest I should work on next?

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Try every one before you check the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'reflection' mean?
practice.answer: Reflection means thinking honestly about how you learn and how your ideas change, so that you can improve. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Reflection is about how you learn, not only ______ you learn.
practice.answer: What (how you learn, not only what you learn).

practice.prompt: True or false: changing your mind after hearing good reasons is a sign of weak thinking.
practice.answer: False. Changing your mind when you meet good reasons is a sign of a strong, open mind.

practice.prompt: An area for ______ is something you are still working to get better at.
practice.answer: Development (an area for development, sometimes called an area for improvement).

practice.prompt: What is a personal perspective?
practice.answer: A personal perspective is your own point of view, shaped by who you are, where you live, and what matters to you.

practice.prompt: Name one benefit of teamwork.
practice.answer: Any one of: more ideas, shared workload, mutual support, combining strengths, work finished faster.

practice.prompt: Name one challenge of teamwork.
practice.answer: Any one of: disagreement over ideas, conflict over who does what, personality clashes, an absent or uncommitted member.

practice.prompt: A good improvement target is small, clear, and you can ______ when you have reached it.
practice.answer: Tell (or measure) when you have reached it.

practice.prompt: Which of these helps reflection? (a) rushing to finish (b) keeping a reflection journal (c) copying the answer.
practice.answer: (b) keeping a reflection journal.

practice.prompt: Cambridge objective 4.3 is about how your personal perspective may change after research or after hearing other ______.
practice.answer: Perspectives (hearing other people's perspectives, or doing research).

practice.prompt: In the frame 'Before I thought ... Now I think ... because ...', which word shows the reason your mind changed?
practice.answer: Because (it shows the reason your mind changed).

practice.prompt: What is the difference between a skill you learnt and a skill you improved?
practice.answer: A skill you learnt is quite new to you; a skill you improved is one you could already do a little and are now better at.

practice.prompt: Name the three good moments to reflect: before a task, ______ a task, and after a task.
practice.answer: During (the three moments are before, during and after a task).

practice.prompt: True or false: a reflection journal should record how you learned, not only what you did.
practice.answer: True. A reflection journal records how you learned, not only what you did.

practice.prompt: Teamwork means a group working towards one ______ outcome, supporting each other.
practice.answer: Shared (a shared outcome).

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each reflection word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Reflection
options: A. Your own point of view, shaped by who you are and what matters to you.
B. Thinking honestly about how you learn and how your ideas change, so you can improve.
C. Something you are good at.
D. A small, clear goal you set to improve.
E. A notebook or file where you record what and how you learned.
F. What you personally bring to a team's shared outcome.
practice.answer: B — Thinking honestly about how you learn and how your ideas change, so you can improve.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Personal perspective
practice.answer: A — Your own point of view, shaped by who you are and what matters to you.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Target
practice.answer: D — A small, clear goal you set to improve.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Contribution
practice.answer: F — What you personally bring to a team's shared outcome.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Personal strength
practice.answer: C — Something you are good at.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Reflection journal
practice.answer: E — A notebook or file where you record what and how you learned.

reflection.prompt: Yasmin says, 'I used to think girls should leave school early, but after interviewing an older student I changed my mind.' Which reflection skill is Yasmin showing?
reflection.modelAnswer: Yasmin is showing how her personal perspective changed after hearing another person (objective 4.3).

reflection.prompt: Karim writes in his journal, 'I learn best when I see one example first.' Is this a helper or a blocker for his learning?
reflection.modelAnswer: It is a helper. Seeing an example first helps Karim learn, so he should use it on purpose.

reflection.prompt: In a team task, Nora did all her own work but never spoke to the others until the end. Was this good teamwork? Explain.
reflection.modelAnswer: No. Real teamwork means working together and supporting each other, not working alone and joining parts only at the end.

reflection.prompt: Theo sets this target: 'I will be better at everything.' What is wrong with it, and how could he fix it?
reflection.modelAnswer: 'I will be better at everything' is too vague to act on. A stronger target names one clear thing, such as: I will ask for help within five minutes of getting stuck.

reflection.prompt: Amara says, 'Before, I thought solar power was too expensive. Now I think it could work here.' What one word is missing that would make this a full reflection?
reflection.modelAnswer: The missing word is 'because'. Amara should say why her view changed, for example: because I learned solar panel prices have fallen.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...
Working with my teacher and classmates in live sessions ...
Asking a family member or neighbour ...
Writing my thoughts in my reflection journal as I went ...

How far you have moved towards a goal.
Deciding on a small, clear goal to help yourself improve.

mistakes: Only saying whether you enjoyed a task, instead of how you learned.
Being unkind to yourself and listing only what went wrong.
Being too easy on yourself and never naming anything to improve.
Saying your view changed but never explaining the 'because'.
Setting a target so vague, like 'be better', that you cannot act on it.
Reflecting in your head but never writing it down, so the learning is lost.
Blaming teammates without looking honestly at your own contribution.
